claim: In cortical models with a single inhibitory neuron class, network stabilization and gain control work in opposition to one another, meaning high gain coincides with low stability and vice versa.
source_text: In cortical models with a single inhibitory neuron class, network stabilization and gain control work in opposition to one another – meaning high gain coincides with low stability and vice versa.
evidence_reasoning: This claim draws from established understanding of single-inhibitory-class cortical models and is supported by logical inference from the modeling literature.

claim: In E – PV – SOM recurrently connected networks, SOM-mediated modulation can lead to simultaneous increases in neuronal gain and network stability.
source_text: We show how, in E – PV – SOM recurrently connected networks, SOM-mediated modulation can lead to simultaneous increases in neuronal gain and network stability.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the modeling data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The impact of a modulation mediated by SOM neurons depends critically on circuit connectivity and the network state.
source_text: Our work exposes how the impact of a modulation mediated by SOM neurons depends critically on circuit connectivity and the network state.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is supported by the modeling results showing different outcomes under different connectivity configurations.

claim: The past 22 years have witnessed a newfound appreciation of inhibition diversity.
source_text: While inhibition has been long measured (Lloyd, 1946; Hartline et al., 1956; Eccles et al., 1954), the past 22 years have witnessed a newfound appreciation of its diversity.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to historical work and reflects established scientific consensus about the timeline of inhibition research.

claim: The invention and widespread use of cell-specific labeling and optogenetic control combined with detailed genetic and physiological characterization of cortical interneurons has painted a complex picture of a circuit.
source_text: The invention and widespread use of cell-specific labeling and optogenetic control (Fenno et al., 2011), combined with the detailed genetic and physiological characterization of cortical interneurons (Markram et al., 2004; Jiang et al., 2015) has painted a complex picture of a circuit.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to relevant methodological and characterization studies.

claim: The standard cortical circuit now includes (at a minimum) SOM and PV expressing interneuron classes, with distinct synaptic interactions between these classes as well as with pyramidal neurons.
source_text: The standard cortical circuit now includes (at a minimum) SOM and PV expressing interneuron classes, with distinct synaptic interactions between these classes as well as with pyramidal neurons (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Tremblay et al., 2016; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Jiang et al., 2015; Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence_reasoning: This claim reflects current scientific consensus supported by multiple citations to experimental characterization studies.

claim: Inhibition has been long identified as a physiological or circuit basis for how cortical activity changes depending upon processing or cognitive needs.
source_text: Inhibition has been long identified as a physiological or circuit basis for how cortical activity changes depending upon processing or cognitive needs (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citation and reflects established knowledge in the field.

claim: Inhibition has been implicated in the suppression of neuronal activity.
source_text: Inhibition has been implicated in the suppression of neuronal activity (Adesnik et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2017; Haider et al., 2013; Adesnik, 2017)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Inhibition has been implicated in gain control of pyramidal neuron firing rates.
source_text: gain control of pyramidal neuron firing rates (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016; Katzner et al., 2011; Ferguson and Cardin, 2020; Silver, 2010)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to relevant experimental and review studies.

claim: Inhibition must prevent runaway cortical activity that would otherwise lead to pathological activity.
source_text: However, inhibition must also prevent runaway cortical activity that would otherwise lead to pathological activity (Haider et al., 2013; Ozeki et al., 2009; Veit et al., 2017)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations and reflects established understanding of inhibition's role in network stability.

claim: Cortical models with excitatory and inhibitory neurons have a long history of study.
source_text: Cortical models with excitatory and inhibitory neurons have a long history of study (Wilson and Cowan, 1972; Griffith, 1963).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to foundational modeling work.

claim: Models with just a single inhibitory interneuron class have successfully explained a wide range of cortical behavior.
source_text: Models with just a single inhibitory interneuron class have successfully explained a wide range of cortical behavior; from contrast-dependent nonlinearities in cortical response (Rubin et al., 2015; Ozeki et al., 2009), to the genesis of irregular and variable spike discharge (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Brunel, 2000), to the mechanisms underlying high-frequency cortical network rhythms (Wang, 2010; Bos et al., 2016).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by multiple citations to modeling studies demonstrating various cortical phenomena.

claim: An attractive hypothesis is that distinct interneurons are within-class functionally homogeneous, yet each class performs functions that are distinct from those of the other classes.
source_text: An attractive hypothesis is that distinct interneurons are within-class functionally homogeneous, yet each class performs functions that are distinct from those of the other classes (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Hattori et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence_reasoning: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by citations, representing a theoretical framework rather than established fact.

claim: A prominent example of the division of labor hypothesis is that PV neurons are well-positioned to provide network stability, allowing SOM neurons to modulate the circuit.
source_text: A prominent example of the division of labor hypothesis is that PV neurons are well-positioned to provide network stability (Wang et al., 2004), allowing SOM neurons to modulate the circuit.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citation and represents an inference from the division of labor hypothesis.

claim: There is strong in vivo evidence that SOM interneurons play a critical role in the modulation of cortical response.
source_text: There is strong in vivo evidence that SOM interneurons play a critical role in the modulation of cortical response (Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Yavorska and Wehr, 2016).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Two distinct inhibitory circuit pathways are often considered when disentangling the impact of SOM inhibition on excitatory neuron response: an inhibitory SOM → E pathway or a disinhibitory SOM → PV → E pathway.
source_text: Two distinct inhibitory circuit pathways are often considered when disentangling the impact of SOM inhibition on excitatory neuron (E) response: an inhibitory SOM → E pathway or a disinhibitory SOM → PV → E pathway.
evidence_reasoning: This reflects established conceptual frameworks in the field for understanding SOM circuit effects.

claim: Increased SOM activity resulted in decreased activity in E neurons in studies of layer 2/3 mouse visual cortex.
source_text: Increased SOM activity resulted in decreased activity in E neurons in studies of layer 2/3 mouse visual cortex (Adesnik et al., 2012; Adesnik, 2017).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is directly supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Decreased SOM activity resulted in increased E neuron activity in the piriform cortex.
source_text: Similarly, decreased SOM activity resulted in increased E neuron activity in the piriform cortex (Canto-Bustos et al., 2022)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is directly supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Silencing layer 4 SOM neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex resulted in decreased activity of E neurons.
source_text: For example, silencing layer 4 SOM neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex resulted in decreased activity of E neurons (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is directly supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: The model response is nonlinear, with neurons in each population having an expansive nonlinear transfer function, consistent with many experimental reports.
source_text: The model response is nonlinear, with neurons in each population having an expansive nonlinear transfer function (Figure 1B; top, see Equation 4), consistent with many experimental reports (Priebe and Ferster, 2008; Romero-Sosa et al., 2021).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by the model specification (data) and citations to experimental studies showing consistency.

claim: A tradeoff between the inhibitory and disinhibitory pathway determines the modulatory influence of SOM neurons upon E neuron activity.
source_text: In sum, while the full E – PV – SOM recurrent circuit invokes a multitude of polysynaptic pathways, a tradeoff between the inhibitory and disinhibitory pathway does indeed determine the modulatory influence of SOM neurons upon E neuron activity.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is supported by the mathematical analysis and modeling results presented.

claim: In most primary sensory cortices, sensory stimulus information arrives at E and PV neurons via feedforward connections.
source_text: In most primary sensory cortices, sensory stimulus information arrives at E and PV neurons via feedforward connections (Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citation and reflects established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Gain modulation refers to changes in the sensitivity of neuron activity to changes in a driving input.
source_text: An important feature of cortical computation is gain modulation, which refers to changes in the sensitivity of neuron activity to changes in a driving input (Silver, 2010; Ferguson and Cardin, 2020; Williford and Maunsell, 2006).
evidence_reasoning: This is a definition supported by citations to relevant review and research articles.

claim: Many experimental studies suggest that inhibitory neurons play an important role in gain modulation.
source_text: Many experimental studies suggest that inhibitory neurons play an important role in gain modulation (Ferguson and Cardin, 2020; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to experimental and review studies.

claim: Network gain measures the sensitivity of E rates owing to the activity of the full recurrent circuit in response to a change in input.
source_text: Here, network gain measures the sensitivity of E rates owing to the activity of the full recurrent circuit in response to a change in input.
evidence_reasoning: This is a definition of the network gain measure used in the study.

claim: Unstable firing rate dynamics are typified by runaway activity when recurrent excitation is not stabilized by recurrent inhibition.
source_text: Unstable firing rate dynamics are typified by runaway activity when recurrent excitation is not stabilized by recurrent inhibition (Ozeki et al., 2009; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Wilson and Cowan, 1972; Griffith, 1963).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to foundational modeling work and reflects established understanding.

claim: Stability in a dynamical system is quantified by the real parts of the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix.
source_text: Stability in a dynamical system is quantified by the real parts of the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix.
evidence_reasoning: This is a standard mathematical definition from dynamical systems theory.

claim: If the real parts of all eigenvalues are less than zero, the system is stable.
source_text: If the real parts of all eigenvalues are less than zero, the system is stable.
evidence_reasoning: This is a standard criterion for stability in dynamical systems theory.

claim: In a network without connections between the E – PV network and the SOM population, network gain is largest for high E rates and low PV rates.
source_text: For each E – PV rate pair, we linearize the network dynamics (i.e. determine the cellular gains bX) and compute the network gain via Equation 2 (Figure 3ii). It is immediately apparent that network gain is largest for high E rates and low PV rates.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3ii.

claim: Network dynamics are most stable for large PV and low E neuron rates.
source_text: In a similar fashion, we consider how stability depends on network activity (rE,rP) (Figure 3iii). Network dynamics are most stable for large PV and low E neuron rates.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 3iii.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between network gain and stability, where high gain is accompanied by low stability and vice-versa in networks without SOM feedback.
source_text: In total, we have an inverse relationship between these two network features, where high gain is accompanied by low stability and vice-versa (compare heatmaps Figure 3ii and iii).
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is supported by comparison of the modeling results in Figure 3.

claim: Modulation of the E – PV circuit via feedforward SOM modulation results in an inverse relationship between network gain and stability.
source_text: In sum, our analysis shows that modulation of the E – PV circuit via feedforward SOM modulation results in an inverse relationship between network gain and stability.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is supported by the modeling analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Adding a recurrent connection onto SOM neurons from the E or PV neurons allows network gain and stability to change in the same direction for a SOM modulation.
source_text: In summary, adding a recurrent connection onto SOM neurons from the E (Figure 5) or PV (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) neurons allows network gain and stability to change in the same direction for a SOM modulation.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 5 and its supplement.

claim: E neurons and PV neurons experience very similar types of inputs, with both receiving excitatory drive from upstream areas and both receiving strong recurrent excitation as well as PV- and SOM-mediated inhibition.
source_text: First, E neurons and PV neurons experience very similar types of inputs. Both receive excitatory drive from upstream areas (Tremblay et al., 2016), and both receive strong recurrent excitation, as well as PV- and SOM-mediated inhibition (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to experimental characterization studies.

claim: The symmetry in the synaptic input to E and PV neurons allows PV neurons to dynamically track E neuron activity.
source_text: This symmetry in the synaptic input to E and PV neurons allows PV neurons to dynamically track E neuron activity.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the input symmetry described.

claim: SOM neurons do not connect to other SOM neurons.
source_text: Second, SOM neurons do not connect to other SOM neurons (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Urban-Ciecko et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2015; Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is directly supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The lack of SOM neuron self-inhibition allows a high gain for any top-down modulatory signal to induce a change in E neuron response.
source_text: However, it is precisely the lack of SOM neuron self-inhibition that allows a high gain for any top-down modulatory signal to induce a change in E neuron response.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the circuit properties and modeling results.

claim: There is evidence that optogenetic perturbation of PV neurons can shift E neuron response gain.
source_text: However, there is also evidence for the reverse labor assignment, namely that optogenetic perturbation of PV neurons can shift E neuron response gain (Wilson et al., 2012; Atallah et al., 2012; Seybold et al., 2015)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: SOM neurons can suppress E neuron firing which in principle would also quench runaway E neuron activity.
source_text: and SOM neurons can suppress E neuron firing which in principle would also quench runaway E neuron activity (Adesnik et al., 2012; Adesnik, 2017).

claim: The PV firing rate strongly modulates both gain and stability, often in opposing directions.
source_text: We show that the PV firing rate strongly modulates both gain and stability, often in opposing directions (Figure 4).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Changing the connection strength of the E – PV subcircuit has the largest effect on network gain.
source_text: Similarly, changing the connection strength of the E – PV subcircuit has the largest effect on network gain (Figure 7).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Feedback onto SOM neurons is an important feature to have more flexibility for circuit computation.
source_text: This suggests that feedback onto SOM neurons is an important feature to have more flexibility for circuit computation.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results showing disentanglement of gain and stability.

claim: Network gain depends on firing rates of E, PV, and SOM neurons at the moment of stimulus presentation.
source_text: An interesting observation is that network gain depends on firing rates of E, PV, and SOM neurons at the moment of stimulus presentation (Figure 3ii; Figure 4Aii, Bii, Cii; Figure 5Aii,Bii, Cii).
evidence_reasoning: This observation is supported by the modeling results across multiple figures.

claim: Changes in inhibitory firing rates and changes in the behavioral state of the animal lead to gain modifications.
source_text: Hence any change in input to the circuit can affect the response gain to a stimulus presentation, in line with experimental evidence which suggests that changes in inhibitory firing rates and changes in the behavioral state of the animal lead to gain modifications (Ferguson and Cardin, 2020).
evidence_reasoning: This claim connects the modeling results to experimental evidence via citation.

claim: PV neurons target both the cell bodies and proximal dendrites of both PV and E neurons.
source_text: PV neurons target both the cell bodies and proximal dendrites of both PV and E neurons (Markram et al., 2004; Tremblay et al., 2016; Di Cristo et al., 2004)

source_text: Dendritic inhibition has been shown to gate burst responses in pyramdial neurons greatly reducing cellular gain (Larkum et al., 2004; Mehaffey et al., 2005)

claim: Dendritic inhibition is localized near the synaptic site for E → E coupling.

claim: SOM neurons may be an important modulator not only of cortical response but also of learning.
source_text: This implies that SOM neurons may be an important modulator not only of cortical response but also of learning.

claim: The E – PV – SOM cortical circuit is best characterized in superficial layers of sensory neocortex.
source_text: The E – PV – SOM cortical circuit is best characterized in superficial layers of sensory neocortex (Pfeffer et al., 2013; Tremblay et al., 2016; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016).

claim: Neuronal gain control has a long history of investigation, with mechanisms that are both bottom-up and top-down mediated.
source_text: Neuronal gain control has a long history of investigation (Salinas and Thier, 2000; Ferguson and Cardin, 2020; Williford and Maunsell, 2006), with mechanisms that are both bottom-up (Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001) and top-down (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Ruff et al., 2018) mediated.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to review and research articles.

claim: Early studies of gain control often dichotomized gain modulations into a simple arithmetic where they are classified as either additive (subtractive) or multiplicative (divisive).
source_text: These studies often dichotomized gain modulations into a simple arithmetic where they are classified as either additive (subtractive) or multiplicative (divisive) (Silver, 2010; Williford and Maunsell, 2006).
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations and reflects historical approaches in the field.

claim: Activation and inactivation of PV and SOM neurons had both additive/subtractive and multiplicative/divisive effects on tuning curves in auditory cortex studies.
source_text: However, a pair of studies in the auditory cortex gave a sobering account whereby activation and inactivation of PV and SOM neurons had both additive/subtractive and multiplicative/divisive effects on tuning curves (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016; Seybold et al., 2015)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Optogenetically decreasing SOM activity leads to mostly additive and multiplicative tuning curve changes in the mouse primary auditory cortex.
source_text: Specifically, optogenetically decreasing SOM activity leads to mostly additive and multiplicative tuning curve changes in the mouse primary auditory cortex (Phillips and Hasenstaub, 2016)

source_text: We show that additive/subtractive and multiplicative/divisive changes in tuning properties can strongly depend on the underlying circuit connectivity
